full_judgment: 16. The relevant part of the rule 5(1) (a) necessary for the disposal of these rules is whether the power of detention is available for "maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community". It will be seen in section 2 of the Act that this very expression has been mentioned which has empower the Government to make rules for 'maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community", Again the power of detention in clause (viii) was given for maintenance of supplies and services essential to the life of the community. It will be at once noticed though, enabling power was given for protecting the economic life of Bangladesh in section 2 but the power of detention was not given in clause (viii) for such reason, e.g. for prejudicing the economic and financial interest of the state, It has been created as specific offense as "prejudicial act" Vide rule 2(e), (xii). Rule 18 deals with the offense of smuggling, It is thus clear that the Emergency Powers Rules have been framed for preventive detention and punitive detention, Preventive detention has been considered by the House of Lords in the case of Liversidge Vs. Anderson (1942 Appeal Case, 206) as a detention of a person without trial in such circumstances that the evidence in possession of the authority is not sufficient to make a legal charge or to secure the conviction of the detenu by legal proof but yet materials are sufficient to justify his detention. On the other hand, the objective of punitive detention is to punish a person for what he has done. The Indian Supreme Court has noticed in the case of Gopalan and Vs. State of Madras, reported in A.I.R. 1950 (SC) 27 that a person is punitively detained only after a trial for committing a crime and after his guilt has been established in a competent Court. It was further observed that preventive detention is not a punitive but precautionary measure. The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept him before he does it and prevent him from doing it. No offense is proved nor any charge formulated and the justification is suspicion or reasonable probability and not criminal conviction which can only be warranted by legal evidence.
